content: Indication-specific dosing for Rosmarinus officinalis Linn (rosemary) includes the application of 1-1 mL of a 6-10% essential oil solution, massaged into the scalp for 2 minutes. This is used for various conditions such as bronchial asthma, peptic ulcers, prostate disorders, inflammatory diseases, liver toxicity, atherosclerosis, stroke, ischemic heart disease, cataracts, leukemia, and sperm motility issues. Rosemary also exhibits anticancer and antitumor properties, enhances mental function and memory, and is used for dyspepsia, hypertension, and rheumatism. It is known to promote menstrual flow and acts as an antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral agent. The German Commission E has approved rosemary for the treatment of dyspepsia, hypertension, alopecia, and rheumatism. However, ingestion of large amounts of rosemary can lead to stomach and intestinal irritation, kidney damage, seizures, toxicity, coma, vomiting, and pulmonary edema. It also has emmenagogue and abortifacient properties, making it potentially unsafe during pregnancy if consumed in doses higher than those found in food. Rosemary is generally considered safe as a food ingredient during pregnancy, but its safety and efficacy in medicinal doses during pregnancy and lactation remain unknown. It is classified as Pregnancy Category A, meaning controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk. However, it is advised to avoid dosages above those found in food due to the lack of sufficient safety data. Rosemary may pose a risk of autoimmune diseases and allergic contact dermatitis, although it is not generally considered a human sensitizer. It has convulsant and epileptogenic properties, which may induce seizures. For lactation, there is no available data regarding its safety.
